 The live engine above runs daily on the server. This second table is the offline TimesFM artifact; it refreshes when the offline pipeline runs and is blended into the live forecasts while fresh.
 How to read this page
 Every symbol gets the same treatment: up to ten years of daily closes go into
 Google TimesFM 2.5 (200M parameters, zero shot) , which emits a 5 session forecast path. "Next %" is the
 forecast for the next trading session versus the latest close; "5 session %" is the horizon end forecast.
 Direction hit is the model's one session ahead direction accuracy over the last 10 sessions for that symbol,
 and RMSE % is its typical size of error relative to price; smaller is better. The small line charts show the
 last 60 sessions of closes. Every label on this page that might be unfamiliar links to the glossary .
 These are offline artifacts , refreshed by the documented procedure in the README; the 800 MB
 model checkpoint cannot run inside the serverless runtime. Each row carries its own as of date, and the
 age of the artifact is shown in the header. Forecasts are model outputs, not advice.
 Zero shot models do not know about earnings dates, guidance or news. Past accuracy never guarantees future accuracy.

title: The models
text:
Models: LSTM, TimesFM and the adaptive ensemble | Premarket India 
 Skip to content 
 Premarket India daily intelligence before the 09:15 open 
 Dashboard 
 Stocks 
 Models 
 Methodology 
 Glossary 
 ELI5 
 Privacy 
 Report Models · 9 min read 
 The models
 What it is, how it was trained, how it is validated, and where it fails.
 Origin
 The forecaster is a faithful implementation of the 3 layer LSTM stock model from the DataCamp tutorial
 “LSTM Stock Prediction with TensorFlow in Python” (Jaa_smb, September 2019). The tutorial's training code
 was rebuilt and executed on the exact stack it specifies, Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.6, because the model uses
 tf.contrib.rnn , which does not exist in TensorFlow 2.x. The training environment was compiled from source
 (OpenSSL 1.1.1w, libffi 3.3, CPython 3.6.15) in this project's sandbox.
 Architecture
 Input mid price = (High + Low) / 2, MinMax scaled per 2,500 row window; last fitted window frozen for inference 
 Cells 3 stacked tf.contrib.rnn.LSTMCell layers: 200 → 200 → 150 units, Xavier initialized kernels, zero initialized biases, forget bias 1.0 added at run time (TF 1.6 semantics) 
 Training truncated BPTT, 50 unrollings, batch 500, Adam 1e-4 with staircase decay (×0.5), gradient clipping 5.0, dropout 0.8 (train only), 30 epochs, mid epoch validation MSE on the test split 
 Output head dense 150 → 1, trained on one session ahead scaled mid prices 
 Inference JS port of the LSTMCell math; warm start with 49 real observations, predict session t+1 , then feed predictions back for a 5 session path (same protocol as the article) 
 Footprint ~693k float32 parameters, shipped as a base64 blob (~2.8 MB) and decoded once per cold start; a full 10 step forecast takes 1 to 2 seconds in Node 
 Training data
 NIFTY 50 (^NSEI) : 4,682 daily bars, 17 Sep 2007 to 16 Oct 2026, fetched from the Yahoo Finance chart API.
 Train/test split at row 4,382, leaving the most recent 300 sessions as a never trained on test region.
 Scaler window : the frozen MinMax scaler covers roughly Aug 2017 → mid 2025, so current index levels sit
 inside the trained range (a runtime guard flags forecasts if prices ever drift outside it).
 Validation against the article
 The same training script was first run on the article's own dataset, HPQ daily bars 1970 to 2017 (12,076 rows,
 split 11,000, exactly as published). The result: test MSE 0.00245 at epoch 30, best 0.00231 , against the
 article's reported range of roughly 0.0023 to 0.0025. The dashboard's article exhibit panel renders the TF session's
 own final epoch predictions for that run, exported directly from TensorFlow, not recomputed in JavaScript.
 The JavaScript inference engine is validated separately: for each exported model it must reproduce TensorFlow's
 10 step sampling output for the article's warm start windows within 5×10⁻³ (float64 JS vs float32 TF). The validation
 harness ships with the project ( tools/validate-lstm.mjs ).
 Live backtest protocol
 Every daily run computes a rolling backtest over the most recent 10 sessions: for each day the model is
 warm started on the 49 real observations ending two days prior, predicts one session ahead, and the error and
 direction hit are recorded. These numbers appear on the dashboard next to the forecast, so the model is judged
 continuously rather than once.
 Limitations, read before trusting anything
 Multi step paths widen in error quickly. The one session ahead number is the meaningful one; sessions 3 to 5 are directional context only.
 The model sees only price history (mid prices). It is blind to news, RBI policy, elections and overnight gaps. That is exactly why the four rule based checks, the context panel, and since October 2026 the daily news and earnings layer (headlines, earnings dates and event flags on the dashboard and stocks page) exist alongside it: the world is shown to you, not silently blended into the numbers.
 Weights are frozen at training time. If NIFTY drifts far outside the scaler range the site flags the forecast as unreliable; the fix is retraining, which is a documented, repeatable procedure in this project.
 A backtest on 10 sessions is small sample. It is evidence of sanity, not of edge.
 Not investment advice. This model is research tooling published with full provenance so its
 claims can be checked. Do not trade on it alone.
 Second model: Google TimesFM (offline)
 Alongside the LSTM, the project runs TimesFM 2.5 (200M parameters) , Google Research's open source
 time series foundation model, pretrained on roughly 100 billion time points, as a zero shot second opinion on the same NIFTY
 series. TimesFM never trains on our data; it forecasts directly from context, which makes it an independent
 reference: when two very different architectures agree, the forecast carries more weight; when they disagree,
 that disagreement is itself information.
 Checkpoint: google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch via the timesfm PyPI package.
 Protocol: last 1,024 daily closes as context, input normalization on, positivity inference on; a 5 session
 forward path and a rolling one session ahead backtest over the same window the LSTM is scored on.
 Runs offline (the ~800 MB checkpoint does not fit a serverless function); results are published as a static
 artifact and stamped with their as of date. The dashboard flags the analysis once it goes stale.
 Refresh procedure is documented in the project README (one venv, one script).
 Why two models? The LSTM is the article's architecture running live in the scan; TimesFM is a
 foundation model cross check. Neither is assumed correct; the dashboard shows both backtests so you can weigh them yourself.
 Third layer: the adaptive ensemble (primary forecast)
 The forecast the dashboard leads with is neither model alone. It is a learned blend :
 ensemble(t+1) = w · TimesFM(t+1) + (1−w) · (LSTM(t+1) − bias) 
 The weight w and the LSTM's bias correction are not chosen by hand. They are found by grid search offline over a
 250 session (~1 year) walk forward window in which both models predicted every session one step ahead using only
 the data that existed beforehand, with no leakage. The parameters that would have minimised RMSE over that year are the ones
 shipped. On the current window TimesFM dominates, so w lands near 1; the second half of the window leans slightly more on
 the LSTM than the first half, which is exactly the drift the weight is relearned to track.
 And it keeps learning after deployment. Every 09:00 IST scan records its prediction in a model scorecard
 (Netlify blobs). When the session prints, the entry is scored against the actual close. Once five sessions have resolved,
 the live w and bias are relearned from the most recent 30 resolved sessions and used for the next morning's blend.
 the offline parameters remain the fallback. The dashboard shows both the provenance of the current weight and the recent
 scorecard rows with each model's error.
 Freshness guard: the TimesFM component is only blended while its artifact is ≤5 sessions old; otherwise the report
 honestly falls back to the bias corrected LSTM and says so on the dashboard.
 Everything is reported with measured walk forward numbers: no in sample flattery, no fabricated accuracy.
 Per stock forecasts (US, global, India ADRs)
 The Stocks page applies the same TimesFM checkpoint, zero shot, to ~50 major symbols:
 US mega caps and sector leaders, SPY/QQQ/DIA benchmark ETFs, global ADRs and Indian ADRs (listed on the NYSE, USD). Each symbol
 gets a 5 session forward path plus a 10 session one session ahead backtest (direction hit and % RMSE) computed in one
 batched offline run; the page is searchable and sortable, and every row carries its own as of date. The refresh procedure
 lives in the README alongside the NIFTY one.
 Provenance of the shipped artifact
 Training script: the tutorial's pipeline, parameterized only where pandas 1.1.5 / numpy 1.19 required it
 ( .as_matrix() → .values ), with an export epilogue added. Deviations documented in the project.
 Exported artifacts: all trainable variables ( multi_rnn_cell/lstm_cell*/kernel|bias , w , b ),
 the frozen scaler min/max, final EMA state, TF reference predictions, and per epoch test MSE.
 Packed for the web as float32 little endian base64 ( tools/pack_model.py ), decoded by lib/lstm.mjs .

title: Methodology
text:
Methodology: the decision framework, sources and FAQ | Premarket India 
 Skip to content 
 Premarket India daily intelligence before the 09:15 open 
 Dashboard 
 Stocks 
 Models 
 Glossary 
 ELI5 
 Methodology 
 Privacy 
 Report Methodology · 11 min read 
 Methodology
 Everything the dashboard shows, and how it is produced.
 Schedule
 Four scheduled runs cover a full day. At 08:40 IST (03:10 UTC) the news cycle collects headlines, earnings
 dates and event flags; at 09:00 IST (03:30 UTC) the premarket scan builds the opening bias;
 at 09:10 IST (03:40 UTC) the per stock engine resolves the latest United States closes and relearns every
 stock's own corrections (Monday to Saturday, so the Friday US close is caught on Saturday); and at 09:20 IST 
 (03:50 UTC) a confirmation pass records what price action actually did after the bell, resolves the opening bias call
 and appends everything to the same report. Each typically finishes in under three minutes. The Run scan now button
 triggers the premarket pipeline on demand (rate limited to once per 2 minutes). Every run overwrites “latest” and
 appends to the dated archive; 400 days of history are kept.
 The decision framework (roles, not equal votes)
 Earlier versions of this tool counted green vs red indicators as ±1 votes. That was wrong, and it is gone.
 The four inputs measure different things and are weighted accordingly:
 Indicator What it actually tells you Role 
 GIFT Nifty (NSE International Exchange, which replaced SGX Nifty in July 2023) 
 Where the Indian market may open relative to its previous close Primary opening indication 
 NASDAQ / Dow Jones + live US futures 
 How US markets performed overnight; futures are the more recent information Global context 
 India VIX 
 The options market's expectation of volatility over the next 30 calendar days Risk assessment, never direction 
 Advances vs declines 
 Whether rising or falling stocks dominate Trend confirmation once trading begins 
 NSE pre open session (09:00 to 09:15) 
 Indicative equilibrium opening level from actual domestic order flow Domestic cross confirmation 
 Step 1: establish the opening bias from GIFT Nifty
 The implied gap is GIFT Nifty's level vs the previous NIFTY 50 close, and its size matters, not just its
 colour: below 0.15% is neutral, 0.15 to 0.5% is a modest gap, above 0.5% is a strong gap. A tiny positive move is not
 equivalent to a substantial one. It remains an estimate, because GIFT is a futures contract carrying basis, not a
 guaranteed opening price.
 Step 2: check whether global markets support the bias
 The previous US session's close and live US index futures (S&P, Nasdaq, Dow) are read as separate inputs,
 alongside the Asian session. If GIFT Nifty indicates a positive open while US futures fall and Asia is weak, the
 framework reports conflicting evidence rather than flipping to a bearish call. Global cues are context;
 they do not automatically override the domestic price discovery that GIFT Nifty and the pre open session represent.
 Step 3: cross confirm with the NSE pre open session
 Between 09:00 and 09:15 the NSE runs order entry and matching, publishing indicative opening levels. The framework
 compares that indication with GIFT Nifty's: agreement confirms the bias; disagreement produces an explicit
 conflicting signals, no directional conclusion classification. When the feed is unreachable
 (nseindia.com blocks datacenter IPs), the report says so and simply loses domestic confirmation. It never invents it.
 Step 4: confirm the trend after the open
 From 09:15, breadth earns its job: whether the index holds above or below its opening price, and whether advancers
 or decliners dominate. The 09:20 IST confirmation pass records the actual open, the last price vs open, live breadth
 and live VIX. These are opening bias classifications and early confirmations, not predictions of the whole session;
 a market can open 0.5% higher and fall all day.
 Step 5: use India VIX for risk, not direction
 A VIX of 18 does not mean bearish, and 14 does not mean calm in absolute terms. The report reads VIX against its
 own trailing 1 year distribution: below the 25th percentile is low, 25 to 60 moderate, 60 to 85 elevated, above 85 high.
 Elevated VIX alongside a bullish bias means “manage risk harder”, not “expect a fall”.
 Two questions, kept separate
 Question A: will the market open higher or lower? Answered by the GIFT gap, cross confirmed by the NSE
 pre open, contextualised by global cues. This is what the headline classification is.
 Question B: will the move sustain after the open? Judged from the post open confirmation snapshot, live
 breadth, and the session's own price action. The LSTM/TimesFM forecasts are inputs to this question, with all their
 caveats on the model page .
 Worked scenarios (how conflicts resolve)
 Observation A B C 
 GIFT Nifty Positive Positive Negative 
 NSE pre open Positive Negative Negative 
 Global cues Positive Mixed Negative 
 India VIX Elevated Low Elevated 
 Report says Positive opening bias, confirmed; risk elevated Conflicting signals, no directional conclusion Negative opening bias; risk elevated 
 Scenario B is the whole point: two greens, a red and a neutral would have counted “bullish” under the
 old vote rule, but the domestic pre open disagrees, so the only honest output is to wait for more information.
 Legacy score
 The old ±1 equal vote score (−5 to +5) is still computed and stored in each report for archive continuity, but the
 dashboard and headlines lead with the framework classification above. History entries made before the change show
 their original scores.
 Implied open
 GIFT Nifty's current level minus NIFTY 50's previous close, as a percentage. Caveat, stated on every report:
 GIFT is a futures contract: the gap includes the futures basis (interest, dividends, time to expiry), so it is an
 indication of the open, not a prediction of it.
 Market context & interpretation thresholds
 Factor Symbol Threshold for a “read” plain language rule 
 Crude oil (WTI / Brent) CL=F, BZ=F ±1% 
 Up → import bill headwind for OMCs, paints, tyres, aviation; tailwind for ONGC/Oil India. Down → the reverse. 
 USD/INR INR=X ±0.2% 
 Rupee weakness → FII outflow pressure and costlier imports; strength → the reverse; IT exporters benefit from weakness. 
 Gold GC=F ±0.5% Up → risk off tone; down → risk on tone. 
 US 10 year yield ^TNX ±5 bp 
 Rising yields → pressure on rate sensitive sectors (banks, realty, autos); falling → relief. Displayed in % (value/10); change in basis points. 
 Asia Pacific ^N225, ^HSI ±0.3% Directional tone for the Indian open from the nearest open markets. 
 S&P 500 spot ^GSPC directional Cross check of the CNBC index quotes. 
 Each factor card shows a 5 day sparkline from Yahoo's spark API; percentages are vs the previous
 session's chart close. These reads are heuristics, labelled as such, not model output.
 LSTM forecast
 The 5 session NIFTY path and its rolling 10 session backtest come from the 3 layer LSTM described on the
 model page . The forecast panel additionally guards itself: if the last 60 scaled price
 points fall outside [−0.05, 1.05] of the frozen training scaler, the panel displays an unreliable, retrain now warning
 instead of pretending the numbers are valid.
 Per stock adaptive engine (every symbol learns)
 Since October 2026 every stock on the stocks page is forecast by a
 gradient boosted tree model trained on a decade of daily data (December 2016 to October 2026,
 about 123,000 training rows over 50 symbols), and every stock then improves on its own results:
 Inputs beyond price history. Each forecast uses 26 features: the stock's own returns, volatility,
 moving average distances, RSI and volume; the market via SPY, QQQ and the CBOE VIX (level, change and one year
 percentile); and the stock's sector via its sector ETF. It is not a single price equation.
 Daily learning loop. After each United States session closes, the engine resolves its pending
 predictions against what really happened. Each stock keeps its own scorecard and relearns three things daily:
 a bias correction (rolling mean of its own recent errors), a
 prediction band width (recalibrated so the stated 80% range keeps
 its promise), and a per stock blend weight with the offline TimesFM artifact, learned exactly like the
 NIFTY ensemble weight.
 Walk forward by year. The training was validated by training one model per year using only earlier
 years, so every score in the decade table on the stocks page is out of sample.
 What honestly improves and what does not. The per stock corrections measurably improve calibration
 (the 80% range covered 78% of outcomes in a day by day 2026 simulation) and shift direction accuracy by about a
 point. Next session direction itself stays near 50 to 53% for every fairly tested model on public data, this one
 included; published academic results cluster at 53 to 58%, and higher claims usually let future information leak
 into the test. This site will not display a direction accuracy number that its own scorecard has not produced.
 The news and events layer (what the models do not read)
 Since October 2026 a separate cycle runs at 08:40 IST , before the premarket scan: it collects market
 headlines (CNBC top news and Google News, United States and India), per stock headlines for all 50 symbols, and the
 next ten days of earnings dates from the Nasdaq calendar. Headlines are tagged with simple keyword rules
 (earnings, merger, lawsuit, regulator, layoffs, rates, inflation, geopolitics, election, cyber, recall, accident)
 and per stock daily headline counts are recorded, so a sudden burst of news is flagged as heavy news . All of
 it is shown on the dashboard and the stocks page with its as of date and source states.
 This layer deliberately stays outside the forecast models. The models would need years of paired news history to
 learn from headlines honestly, and we will not pretend otherwise: today the news is displayed for you to weigh,
 and the daily counts accumulate in a blob so a future model version can be trained on them for real.
 Sources & integrity policy
 CNBC : quote.cnbc.com/quote-html-webservice/restQuote for .IXIC , .DJI , .SPX class symbols.
 Yahoo Finance : chart v8 ( ^INDIAVIX , ^NSEI , context symbols) and spark v7 (breadth constituents, at most 20 symbols per call).
 NSE India : market status and advance decline endpoints, tried first for breadth; frequently blocks datacenter IPs, hence the Yahoo fallback.
 TradingView : GIFT Nifty daily bar close and change from the public symbol page (server rendered state), the only reliable route found from cloud functions.
 Known blocked sources (investing.com, nseindia.com pages from cloud IPs, moneycontrol, Alpha Vantage free tier)
 are not silently substituted: when the primary fails, the row shows the fallback source that actually answered, or
 the word unavailable. Prices may be delayed by up to 15 to 20 minutes depending on the provider.
 FAQ
 When exactly is the report generated?
 Twice per trading day: 09:00 IST (premarket report) and 09:20 IST (post open confirmation appended to the same report). Manual runs from the dashboard button are possible any time and are rate limited to one per two minutes.
 What happens on weekends and exchange holidays?
 Weekends are skipped by the scheduler (in IST, not UTC). Exchange holidays are not modelled: the scan still runs and reports the latest available session values, each labelled with its own session date, so nothing pretends to be “today's” data.
 Why do some checks show “unavailable” instead of a number?
 Because the source failed or blocked the request. The check is then excluded from the score. Inventing or carrying forward a stale value silently would be worse than admitting the gap.
 Can I get the raw data?
 Yes: /api/latest (JSON of the newest report), /api/history (index of saved dates), /api/report?date=YYYY-MM-DD&format=json|md|html for any archived day, and /assets/model-analysis.json for the current LSTM vs TimesFM comparison.
 Is this investment advice?
 No. It is a research tool showing what public data said before the open, with sources, timestamps and honest error bars. Do your own diligence.
 How often is the model retrained?
 Weights ship frozen with the deployment. The documented retraining procedure (same script, refreshed NIFTY CSV, repack) is part of the project; the dashboard flags when prices drift out of the trained scaler range, which is the trigger to retrain.

title: This site, explained like you are five
text:
ELI5: this site explained like you are five | India Premarket Intelligence 
 Skip to content 
 Premarket India daily intelligence before the 09:15 open 
 Dashboard 
 Stocks 
 Models 
 Methodology 
 Glossary 
 ELI5 
 Privacy 
 Report ELI5 · 7 min read 
 This site, explained like you are five
 Simple words first. Every blue word links to the glossary , which has the exact grown up definition.
 What is this website?
 Every morning at 9 o'clock, before the Indian stock market wakes up, this website writes a short report. The report
 says: here is how the market will probably start today. Up, down, or flat. And here is how sure we are.
 Think of it like a weather report, but for the stock market instead of the sky.
 What is the NIFTY 50?
 Imagine the 50 biggest shops in one big market. Someone adds up how all 50 shops are doing every day and turns it
 into one score. That score is called the NIFTY 50 . When people say the market
 went up today, they usually mean this score went up.
 What happens before the market opens?
 The market sleeps at night. It wakes at 9:15 in the morning. But before it wakes, there are already clues about
 whether it will start in a good mood or a bad mood. This website collects those clues at 9:00, fifteen minutes
 before the bell.
 There is even a warm up round from 9:00 to 9:15 called the pre open
 session , where everyone places their first orders without trading yet. It is like kids lining up before the school
 gate opens.
 The clues we check
 Clue 1: the practice price. While India sleeps, a copy of the NIFTY is already being traded far away, in a
 place called GIFT City in Gujarat and on exchanges abroad. That price is called GIFT
 Nifty . It is like a practice vote about where the market will open. It is our most important clue.
 Clue 2: how the world slept. While India slept, America's markets finished their day and Japan and Hong Kong
 were already trading. If they had a bad night, India often starts grumpy too. We also check the price of
 oil (India buys a lot of it), gold , and a few other
 things. These are the market context . They set the mood. They do not give
 orders.
 Clue 3: the fear thermometer. It is called India VIX . It does not say
 up or down. It says how bumpy the road is expected to be today. A high number means hold on tight, in either
 direction.
 Clue 4: counting hands. After the market opens, we count how many stocks went up (hands raised) and how many
 went down (hands down). If the market goes up but most hands are down, something is fishy. This clue comes a little
 later, at 9:20, in the post open check .
 Sometimes the clues disagree. Then we say so, out loud: conflicting
 signals , no clear answer today. Guessing anyway would be lying to you.
 The computer that guesses the price
 Alongside the clue reading, a computer program guesses tomorrow's NIFTY number. Actually there are two.
 The student. One program, called an LSTM , studied almost 20 years of old
 NIFTY numbers, the way a student studies old exam papers. It learned patterns in how the numbers move one day after
 the next.
 The well read outsider. The other program, TimesFM , was trained by
 Google on about a hundred billion numbers from all kinds of things, and it has never studied our NIFTY homework. It
 just looks at our recent numbers and gives an opinion. That is fair, because it cannot cheat.
 The blend. We ask both, then combine their answers into one number called the
 ensemble . How much do we trust each one? We measured. Over the last year of
 guessing one day ahead, the outsider was right far more often, so it gets almost all the say, and the student gets a
 small say. The exact share is a number called w , and it is set by the
 measurements, not by us.
 How the computer learns from its mistakes
 Every morning the website writes down its guess in a notebook called the
 scorecard . The next day, when the real answer is out, it checks: how wrong were
 we? Each model gets its mistake written down, like marks on a report card. After enough days, the share of trust
 between the two guessers is recalculated from the recent marks. If the student starts doing better, its say grows.
 All by itself, every day.
 The important part: we show you the marks. Every accuracy number on this site was measured on days the models had
 never seen while learning. Nobody here can see the future. We are just very honest about the odds.
 The page with 50 stocks
 There is also a page, Stocks , where the well read outsider program guesses the next few
 days for 50 famous companies: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Toyota, an Indian bank or two, and more. Each guess comes
 with its own little track record, so you can see how often that guessing worked for that stock lately.
 What this site cannot do
 Its number guessing does not read the news. That is why, every morning at 08:40, the site also collects real
 headlines for every stock, checks who reports earnings this week, and flags big words like war, election, lawsuit,
 recall or rate cut. It shows these next to the numbers instead of hiding them inside the math, so you can weigh
 what the equations cannot see.
 It cannot promise. Next day direction is genuinely hard: out of sample, honest models land only a little above
 half right, and stock prices are noisy. Anyone who promises you certain market predictions is not telling
 the truth.
 It is not advice. It is a measurement instrument: it reads clues and shows its own track record. What you do with
 it is up to you.
 Where to go next
 Ready for the grown up versions? The glossary defines every word used on this site.
 The methodology page explains exactly how every number is produced. The
 models page shows how the two guessers work and how they scored. And the
 dashboard is the daily report itself.

 Privacy policy
 Last updated: 17 October 2026
 The short version
 No accounts. No cookies. No analytics. No advertising. No third party trackers.
 The only thing stored in your browser is one localStorage key remembering your light/dark theme choice.
 What we collect
 Nothing personal. The site is static pages plus serverless functions that fetch public market data.
 We do not ask for your name, email, or any identifier, and we do not fingerprint your device.
 Server logs
 The hosting platform (Netlify) keeps standard request logs (IP address, user agent, timestamp) for security and
 abuse prevention, as described in Netlify's own privacy policy. We do not access, analyze, or sell these logs.
 Local storage
 pm-theme : your theme preference (“light” or “dark”). Stored in your browser only; never transmitted to us.
 Clearing your browser storage removes it. No other client side storage is used.
 Third party data providers
 Market data is fetched server side by our cloud functions from CNBC, Yahoo Finance, NSE India and
 TradingView. Your browser never contacts these providers through this site, and they do not receive your IP from us.
 Displayed data remains the property of its providers and is shown for research purposes only.
 Children
 The site is a financial research tool, not directed at children, and collects no data from anyone.
 Changes
 If this policy changes materially (for example, if analytics were ever added; they won't be without a policy
 update first), this page and its “last updated” date will change before the feature ships.

title: Glossary: NIFTY 50
text:
NIFTY 50

A report card that averages the scores of India's 50 biggest listed companies.
The main stock index of the National Stock Exchange of India. It tracks the combined value of 50 large Indian companies, so when people say the market went up or down, this number is usually what they mean.

title: Glossary: NSE (National Stock Exchange)
text:
NSE (National Stock Exchange)


The National Stock Exchange of India, the exchange where NIFTY 50 companies trade. Its regular session runs from 09:15 to 15:30 India time.

title: Glossary: Index
text:
Index


A single number built from many stocks so that the whole market can be tracked at a glance. The NIFTY 50, the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones are all indexes.

title: Glossary: Pre open session
text:
Pre open session


The 15 minute window from 09:00 to 09:15 India time in which NSE collects orders before regular trading starts. The collected orders produce an opening price at 09:15. We read it as a cross check on the opening gap.

title: Glossary: Premarket
text:
Premarket


The time before a market opens. For the Indian market this report is produced at 09:00 India time, 15 minutes before the bell.

title: Glossary: Opening gap
text:
Opening gap

How far the market jumps up or down the moment it wakes up, compared with where it slept.
The difference between yesterday's closing price and today's opening price. A gap up means the market opens above the last close. A gap down means it opens below. Our bands: neutral is under 0.15 percent, modest is under 0.50 percent, strong is 0.50 percent or more.

title: Glossary: Gap tiers (neutral, modest, strong)
text:
Gap tiers (neutral, modest, strong)


Our labels for gap size. Under 0.15 percent the gap is noise. Under 0.50 percent it is a modest tilt. At 0.50 percent or more it is a strong signal worth attention.

title: Glossary: GIFT Nifty
text:
GIFT Nifty

A early preview of the NIFTY price that trades in Gujarat while the main market sleeps.
A futures contract on the NIFTY 50 that trades on the NSE International Exchange at GIFT City, Gujarat. It trades for almost 21 hours a day, so while the Indian market is closed it is the best live hint of where NIFTY will open. It is our primary opening indication.

title: Glossary: NSE IX
text:
NSE IX


The NSE International Exchange at GIFT City, where GIFT Nifty trades.

title: Glossary: Previous close
text:
Previous close


The last traded price of the previous session. The reference point for measuring gaps and daily percentage moves.

title: Glossary: Close and closing price
text:
Close and closing price


The final price of a session. On this site, close usually means the regular session close of the NIFTY 50.

title: Glossary: Open price
text:
Open price


The first price of a session, discovered in the pre open auction at 09:15 India time.

title: Glossary: Mid price
text:
Mid price


The average of a session's high and low, written as (High + Low) / 2. The LSTM model was trained to predict this value for the next session. It is smoother than the close and harder to fake with one large trade.

title: Glossary: Session
text:
Session


One trading day, from open to close. Our forecasts count time in sessions, not calendar days.

title: Glossary: Trading day
text:
Trading day


A day on which the exchange is open. We skip weekends in forecasts. Exchange holidays are not modelled, so a forecast can land on a holiday and roll to the next session in reality.

title: Glossary: Market breadth
text:
Market breadth


How many stocks went up versus down across the whole market. Wide participation confirms a move. A rally on falling breadth is a warning.

title: Glossary: Advances and declines (A/D)
text:
Advances and declines (A/D)


The count of stocks that closed higher (advances) versus lower (declines). We read it after the open to confirm the direction the gap pointed at. It is a confirmation tool, not a premarket predictor.

title: Glossary: India VIX
text:
India VIX

A fear thermometer. It measures how bumpy the road ahead is expected to be, not which way the road slopes.
India's volatility index, computed from NIFTY option prices. It approximates how large the market's swings are expected to be over the next 30 calendar days. High VIX means big expected swings, up or down. It says nothing about direction.

title: Glossary: Risk tiers
text:
Risk tiers


Our labels for the India VIX level compared with its own past year: low is below the 25th percentile, moderate is below the 60th, elevated is below the 85th, high is at or above it.

title: Glossary: Gradient boosted trees
text:
Gradient boosted trees


The model behind the per stock forecasts. It is a team of simple yes no decision trees; each tree fixes a little of what the previous ones got wrong, and their votes are added up. It was trained on a decade of daily data across the 50 stocks plus market and sector context.

title: Glossary: Feature
text:
Feature


One input number a model looks at before making a forecast, for example yesterday's SPY return or how far a stock sits above its 50 day average. The per stock model uses 26 features; price history alone is not the whole picture.

title: Glossary: Prediction band (80%)
text:
Prediction band (80%)


The range around a forecast where the outcome lands about 80 percent of the time. The width is learned per stock from its own recent misses, so a wide band simply means that stock has been hard to call. It is an honest range, not a promise.

title: Glossary: Coverage
text:
Coverage


How often outcomes actually land inside the stated prediction band. An 80 percent band should catch about 80 percent of outcomes over time; the per stock engine measures this again daily and tightens or widens each band to keep the promise.

title: Glossary: Adaptive (self learning)
text:
Adaptive (self learning)


A system that records its own predictions, checks them against what really happened, and changes its own settings as a result. This site does it for the NIFTY blend weight and, per stock, for the bias correction, the band width and the TimesFM blend.

title: Glossary: Hit rate (direction)
text:
Hit rate (direction)


The share of sessions where the model called the direction, up or down, correctly. For next session stock direction with public data, honest scores sit near 50 to 55 percent; anything claiming 90 percent plus on daily direction is not being tested fairly.

title: Glossary: Event risk
text:
Event risk


The chance that a specific happening, like an earnings report, an election, a war or a lawsuit, moves a stock suddenly by more than any pattern in its prices would suggest. The site flags upcoming earnings and heavy news for exactly this reason.

title: Glossary: Earnings date
text:
Earnings date


The day a company reports its quarterly results, usually before the US market opens or after it closes. Stocks often swing hard on the report and the outlook that comes with it, which is why the stocks page shows upcoming dates from the Nasdaq calendar.

title: Glossary: News volume
text:
News volume


How many headlines a stock is generating today compared with its own recent normal. A sudden burst, flagged here as heavy news, often means something real is happening that the price models have not seen yet.

title: Glossary: Percentile
text:
Percentile


A way to rank a value against its own history. The 65th percentile means the current value is higher than 65 percent of the values seen in the comparison window, which we set at one year.

title: Glossary: US indices (Dow, Nasdaq, S&P 500)
text:
US indices (Dow, Nasdaq, S&P 500)


The three main United States stock indexes. Because the US session closes before India opens, their overnight result is a standard input for reading the Indian open.

title: Glossary: US index futures (ES, NQ, YM)
text:
US index futures (ES, NQ, YM)


Contracts that trade around the clock on the future level of the S&P 500 (ES), Nasdaq 100 (NQ) and Dow Jones (YM). In the Indian morning they are live, so they show how traders are positioning right now, not just how yesterday ended.

title: Glossary: Index futures
text:
Index futures


Agreements to buy or sell an index at a set price on a set future date. Because they trade longer hours than the cash market, they act as a live vote on where the index will open.

title: Glossary: Asia session (Nikkei, Hang Seng)
text:
Asia session (Nikkei, Hang Seng)


The Japanese Nikkei 225 and the Hong Kong Hang Seng indexes, trading while the Indian market prepares to open. They are context for how global risk appetite looks this morning.

title: Glossary: Brent crude (oil)
text:
Brent crude (oil)


The world price benchmark for oil. India imports most of its oil, so a sharp move in crude is a standard macro input for Indian markets.

title: Glossary: Gold
text:
Gold


The safe haven metal. Rising gold often pairs with cautious risk appetite. Tracked as context only.

title: Glossary: US 10 year yield
text:
US 10 year yield


The interest rate the United States government pays to borrow for ten years. It is the world's reference rate. A fast rise tends to press risk assets everywhere.

title: Glossary: Dollar Index (DXY)
text:
Dollar Index (DXY)


An index of the US dollar against major currencies. A strong dollar can pull money out of emerging markets such as India.

title: Glossary: USD INR
text:
USD INR


The exchange rate between the US dollar and the Indian rupee. A fast move matters for foreign flows into Indian shares.

title: Glossary: Market context
text:
Market context


The background factors we track alongside the main signals: oil, gold, the US 10 year yield, the dollar, the rupee and the Asia session indexes. Context frames the decision. It never overrides the primary signals.

title: Glossary: ADR (American Depositary Receipt)
text:
ADR (American Depositary Receipt)


A receipt traded on a United States exchange that represents shares of a foreign company. Infosys, Wipro, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank all have ADRs listed in New York, priced in US dollars.

title: Glossary: ETF (exchange traded fund)
text:
ETF (exchange traded fund)


A fund that trades on an exchange like a single stock. SPY, QQQ and DIA track the S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100 and the Dow Jones respectively.

title: Glossary: Candle (5 minute chart)
text:
Candle (5 minute chart)


One block on a price chart showing the open, high, low and close of a short window, here five minutes. The post open check reads 5 minute candles after the bell.

title: Glossary: Post open confirmation
text:
Post open confirmation


The 09:20 India time snapshot that checks what actually happened after the open: the opening price, whether gains are holding, and the live advances and declines count. It closes the loop on the 09:00 read.

title: Glossary: Stance
text:
Stance


Our one word summary of a context factor: supportive, neutral or cautionary. Stances describe evidence. They are not trade instructions.

title: Glossary: Conflicting signals
text:
Conflicting signals


When independent checks disagree, for example GIFT Nifty points down while the pre open session leans up. The honest conclusion is no directional conclusion. We say so instead of forcing a call.

title: Glossary: LSTM
text:
LSTM

A student who studied four thousand days of NIFTY history and learned patterns in the order of the numbers.
Long Short Term Memory, a type of recurrent neural network that reads a sequence step by step and keeps a memory of what it has seen. Our LSTM has three layers of 200, 200 and 150 cells and predicts the next session's mid price of the NIFTY 50. It runs live inside the daily scan.

title: Glossary: TimesFM
text:
TimesFM

A very well read outsider who has seen a million similar number patterns and gives an opinion without studying our specific homework.
Google's open source time series foundation model, version 2.5 with 200 million parameters. It was trained by Google on roughly 100 billion time points and forecasts without any training on our data, which is called zero shot. It runs offline because its checkpoint is about 800 MB and too large for the serverless runtime.

title: Glossary: Foundation model
text:
Foundation model


A large model pretrained once on huge amounts of data and then reused for many tasks with little or no extra training. TimesFM is a foundation model for numeric time series.

title: Glossary: Zero shot
text:
Zero shot


Making forecasts with a model that was never trained on the data in question. TimesFM never saw NIFTY data during its training, so its NIFTY forecasts are zero shot. This makes it an independent second opinion.

title: Glossary: Ensemble
text:
Ensemble

Asking two students and trusting the one with the better track record a bit more, in exact proportion.
A forecast built by combining models. Ours is a weighted blend: ensemble equals w times TimesFM plus (1 minus w) times the bias corrected LSTM. The weight w and the bias are learned from measured errors, not chosen by hand. It is the primary forecast on the dashboard.

title: Glossary: Blend weight (w)
text:
Blend weight (w)


The number between 0 and 1 that sets how much each model contributes to the ensemble. At w equal to 1 the forecast is pure TimesFM. At 0 it is pure corrected LSTM. It is learned by grid search over a walk forward window and relearned live from the scorecard.

title: Glossary: Bias correction
text:
Bias correction


Subtracting a model's average error from its forecasts. If a model is on average 70 points too high, we subtract 70 before using its number. The average is measured on the walk forward window.

title: Glossary: Grid search
text:
Grid search


Trying every candidate value in a range and keeping the one that would have scored best. We search w from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.01. Simple, transparent, and enough for one parameter.

title: Glossary: Walk forward evaluation
text:
Walk forward evaluation

Replaying the year in order, guessing each morning, and only then checking the answers.
A honest way to score a model: predict one session ahead, step forward, predict again, and repeat using only data that existed at each point. Our main window is 250 sessions, about one year. No future information leaks into any prediction.

title: Glossary: Backtest
text:
Backtest


Testing a model on past data to measure how it would have done. Every accuracy number on this site comes from a backtest, and the method matters: see walk forward evaluation.

title: Glossary: RMSE (root mean square error)
text:
RMSE (root mean square error)

On a normal day, how far off the guess is.
The typical size of a model's miss, in index points. Bigger errors count extra because errors are squared before averaging. An RMSE of 209 points means a typical miss of roughly 209 NIFTY points on that window.

title: Glossary: MAE (mean absolute error)
text:
MAE (mean absolute error)


The plain average of the sizes of a model's misses, in index points. Less sensitive to one terrible day than RMSE.

title: Glossary: MSE (mean squared error)
text:
MSE (mean squared error)


The average of squared errors. The training loop of the LSTM minimises this. Our tutorial reproduction reached a test MSE of 0.00243, inside the range the original article reported.

title: Glossary: Direction hit rate
text:
Direction hit rate


The share of sessions where the model predicted the correct direction, up or down, measured against the previous close. A coin flip is 50 percent. Our NIFTY numbers and every per stock number on the stocks page are measured this way.

title: Glossary: One session ahead
text:
One session ahead


A prediction for the very next session only. All walk forward scoring on this site is one session ahead, the hardest honest test.

title: Glossary: Forecast path
text:
Forecast path


The model's predicted prices for the next five sessions, in order. Error grows quickly after the first step or two, so the path is directional context, not a target list.

title: Glossary: Forecast horizon
text:
Forecast horizon


How far ahead a forecast reaches. Our models forecast five sessions.

title: Glossary: Model scorecard
text:
Model scorecard

The models' report card, updated every day, and the lesson they study each night.
The running record of every morning's prediction versus what actually happened. Each scan logs its forecast for the next session. When that session closes, the entry is resolved with the actual price and each model's error. After five resolved sessions the blend weight is relearned from this live evidence.

title: Glossary: Resolved session
text:
Resolved session


A scorecard entry whose session has finished, so the actual price is known and the error can be scored.

title: Glossary: Artifact
text:
Artifact


A file of results produced by an offline run, for example the TimesFM forecast and its backtest numbers. Artifacts carry an as of date. When an artifact is more than five sessions old the ensemble stops using it and says so.

title: Glossary: Stale and fresh
text:
Stale and fresh


Fresh means the data behind a number is recent enough to trust for its purpose. Our rule: the TimesFM artifact must be no more than five sessions old, cached market data must be within its per source time limit, and anything older is either labelled with its age or dropped.

title: Glossary: Data leakage
text:
Data leakage


The classic backtest mistake: letting a model see future information while being scored. It inflates accuracy that then vanishes in real use. Our walk forward protocol exists to prevent it.

title: Glossary: Training and test split
text:
Training and test split


Dividing history so a model learns from one part and is scored on another it never saw. The NIFTY model trains on 4,382 sessions and is scored on the rest.

title: Glossary: Epochs
text:
Epochs


Full passes through the training data. The LSTM trains for 30 epochs, matching the original tutorial.

title: Glossary: Truncated BPTT
text:
Truncated BPTT


Backpropagation through time, truncated: the LSTM is trained by unrolling it over a fixed number of steps (50 for us) and updating weights over that window. This is how the tutorial trains recurrent models on long sequences.

title: Glossary: Unrollings
text:
Unrollings


The number of sequence steps the LSTM looks back at each training step. Our value is 50 sessions.

title: Glossary: EMA (exponential moving average)
text:
EMA (exponential moving average)


A smoothed average that weights recent values more. The tutorial pipeline uses EMA smoothing in its scaling step.

title: Glossary: MinMax scaling
text:
MinMax scaling


Rescaling prices into the range from 0 to 1 so the network can learn stably. Our NIFTY scaler maps 7,774 to 0 and 26,214 to 1. If prices leave that range the forecast is flagged as unreliable until the model retrains.

title: Glossary: Scaler range
text:
Scaler range


The minimum and maximum prices the model was trained on. Prices outside the range produce unreliable outputs, and the dashboard warns when that happens.

title: Glossary: Inference
text:
Inference


Running a trained model on new data to get a prediction. The LSTM does inference in the cloud function in a few milliseconds.

title: Glossary: Parameters
text:
Parameters


The learned numbers inside a model. TimesFM 2.5 has about 200 million of them. The LSTM has roughly 500 thousand.

title: Glossary: Checkpoint
text:
Checkpoint


The saved file of a trained model's parameters. The TimesFM checkpoint is about 800 MB, which is why it runs offline rather than on the website's server.

title: Glossary: Quantile forecast
text:
Quantile forecast


A forecast of a range rather than a single number, for example a low and high band. TimesFM can produce these; we currently publish its point forecast, the middle of the range.

title: Glossary: Data source
text:
Data source


An outside service we fetch market data from. Current sources: CNBC and Yahoo Finance for United States indexes, TradingView for GIFT Nifty, Yahoo Finance for India VIX and NIFTY history, and the Nasdaq public quote API for the per stock page.

title: Glossary: Fallback
text:
Fallback

If the first door is locked, the site tries the next one on its own, and tells you it did.
An automatic backup path when a primary source fails. Each source has alternates where they exist and a last good cache. Switching is automatic and the report says which path was used, so a reader always knows what a number came from.

title: Glossary: Cached data
text:
Cached data


A copy of the last successful fetch, kept in storage with its timestamp. If a source fails, the report can fall back to the cached copy if it is still within that source's freshness limit. Any number served from cache is labelled with its age.

title: Glossary: Rate limit (HTTP 429)
text:
Rate limit (HTTP 429)


A server refusing requests because too many arrived too quickly from one address. Public market APIs do this aggressively. It is why the site keeps multiple sources and paces its requests.

title: Glossary: As of date
text:
As of date


The date a number or dataset was true for. Every artifact and every stock row carries one. An as of stamp is the honest way to publish data that cannot be recomputed continuously.

title: Glossary: Stocks page
text:
Stocks page


The page at /stocks.html with TimesFM forecasts for 50 major symbols: United States mega caps, sector leaders, the SPY, QQQ and DIA index ETFs, global ADRs and Indian ADRs. Each row has its own backtest and as of date.

title: Glossary: Sparkline
text:
Sparkline


A tiny chart without axes that shows the shape of recent prices at a glance. On the stocks page each sparkline covers the last 60 sessions.

title: Glossary: Basis point
text:
Basis point


One hundredth of a percent. 25 basis points is 0.25 percent. Used mainly for rate moves.

title: Glossary: IST and UTC
text:
IST and UTC


IST is India Standard Time, UTC plus 5 hours 30 minutes. UTC is the world clock with no daylight shifts. The report runs at 09:00 IST. Data timestamps from sources are usually UTC.

title: Glossary: ELI5
text:
ELI5


Explain like I am five. Our ELI5 page explains the whole site in the simplest possible words, with everyday comparisons and no jargon.

title: Glossary: API
text:
API


A service a program can call to get data back. This site exposes its own, for example /api/latest returns the newest report as JSON.

title: Glossary: JSON
text:
JSON


A plain text format for structured data that both programs and people can read. Reports and artifacts on this site are stored and served as JSON.

title: Glossary: Endpoint
text:
Endpoint


One address of an API, for example /api/latest or /api/history.

title: Glossary: Serverless function
text:
Serverless function


A small program that runs on demand in the cloud provider's machines and sleeps between runs. The site's scan, report and history pages are serverless functions on Netlify.

title: Glossary: Schedule (cron)
text:
Schedule (cron)


A timed trigger that runs a function automatically. Two are registered: 09:00 India time for the main scan and 09:20 for the post open confirmation, Monday to Friday. Cron is the standard syntax for expressing such times.

title: Glossary: Blob storage
text:
Blob storage


The cloud key value store where reports, the scorecard and data caches are kept. Short for binary large object.

title: Glossary: CSP (Content Security Policy)
text:
CSP (Content Security Policy)


A security rule the site sends with every page that tells the browser which scripts and styles are allowed to run. Ours is strict: only the site's own files plus one exact Netlify widget script, identified by its cryptographic hash.
